cards.front: State the four main objectives of government macroeconomic policy.
cards.back:
• Economic growth.
  • Price stability (low and stable inflation — the UK's 2% CPI target).
  • Minimising unemployment.
  • A stable balance of payments on current account.

Be aware of further objectives too — balancing the government budget, a more equitable distribution of income, and environmental protection — and that the importance attached to each objective changes over time.

cards.front: Give the UK's usual targets for growth, unemployment and inflation, and why each matters.
cards.back:
• Growth — sustainable, around 2–3%: raises incomes, living standards, employment and tax revenue.
  • Unemployment — near full employment, around 4–5%, allowing for frictional unemployment: maximises output and reduces poverty.
  • Inflation — the 2% CPI target: certainty for consumers and firms, protects savings, supports competitiveness.

The current account aim is a sustainable position — only a small surplus or deficit.

cards.front: Why can the macroeconomic objectives conflict, at least in the short run?
cards.back:
Policies that improve one objective often worsen another: stimulating growth and employment raises demand-pull inflation and pulls in imports; squeezing inflation with higher interest rates slows growth and costs jobs.

Governments therefore prioritise, and the priority shifts with circumstances — jobs and demand after 2008, inflation in 2022–23. AQA flags exactly this: the importance attached to objectives changes over time.

cards.front: Distinguish nominal GDP, real GDP and real GDP per capita.
cards.back:
Nominal GDP values output at current prices.

Real GDP adjusts for inflation, valuing output at constant prices — approximately, % change in real GDP = % change in nominal GDP − inflation.

Real GDP per capita divides real GDP by the population: average output per person, the better starting point for living standards.

cards.front: How does the RPI differ from the CPI?
cards.back:
Both track the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services and are used to calculate the inflation rate. The RPI additionally includes housing costs — mortgage interest payments and council tax — which the CPI leaves out.

RPI therefore usually runs higher than CPI, and the CPI is the measure targeted by the Bank of England.

cards.front: State the formulas for the unemployment rate and the employment rate.
cards.back:
The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labour force unemployed and actively seeking work. The employment rate is the percentage of the working-age population in work.

The denominators differ — someone economically inactive is in neither numerator, so the two rates can move independently.
cards.formulaHtml: Unemploymentrate=Unemployed/Labourforce×100Unemployment rate = Unemployed / Labour force × 100Unemploymentrate=Unemployed/Labourforce×100

cards.front: Define the current account of the balance of payments, and name the remaining spec indicator.
cards.back:
The balance of payments records all transactions between a country and the rest of the world; the current account is the part that records trade in goods and services, income flows, and current transfers.

The final indicator on the AQA list is productivity — output per worker (or per hour worked) — which drives long-run growth and competitiveness.

cards.front: Define an index number and the base year.
cards.back:
An index number expresses the value of a variable relative to a chosen base value, which is set equal to 100. The base year is the reference year all others are compared against.

Index numbers turn awkward raw figures — thousands of prices, GDP in billions — into one easy series, and they track not just prices but real GDP, wages, productivity and share prices such as the FTSE 100.

cards.front: State the index number formula, and interpret an index of 115.
cards.back: An index of 115 means the variable is 15% higher than in the base year; an index of 92 means 8% lower. The percentage change reads straight off the index only against the base year — comparing 115 with 105 is a rise of 115 ÷ 105, about 9.5%, not 10 points.

cards.front: Why does the CPI use weights, and what do the 'average family' and the 'basket' mean?
cards.back:
The CPI prices a basket of goods and services chosen to represent the spending of the average family. Each category gets a weight reflecting its share of household spending, so a 10% rise in a heavily-weighted item (housing) moves the index far more than the same rise in a lightly-weighted one (tea bags).

The weighted index is the sum of weight × price index across categories, divided by the total weight.

cards.front: A simplified basket has three categories with weights out of 1,000: housing 400 (price index 108), transport 350 (index 104), food 250 (index 112). Calculate the weighted CPI and interpret it.
cards.back:
Weight × index:

  • Housing 400 × 108 = 43,200
  • Transport 350 × 104 = 36,400
  • Food 250 × 112 = 28,000

Total = 107,600

Divide by total weight: 107,600 ÷ 1,000 = 107.6

Prices across the basket average 7.6% above the base year. Food rose fastest (12%), but the heavily-weighted housing category matters more to the overall index — that is what weighting does.

cards.front: Define national income, and state the national income identity.
cards.back:
National income is the total value of all goods and services produced in an economy over a given period. It can be measured in three equivalent ways — as total output, total income, or total expenditure — because one person's spending is another person's income, and all income is ultimately earned by producing output.

Hence the identity: national output ≡ national income ≡ national expenditure.

cards.front: Distinguish GDP from GNI.
cards.back:
GDP measures the value of everything produced within a country's borders, regardless of who owns the factors of production.

GNI (also called GNP) is GDP plus net income from abroad — income earned by residents from overseas assets, minus income earned by foreign residents from domestic assets. For countries with large overseas holdings or heavy inward investment, the two diverge noticeably.

cards.front: Evaluate the limitations of national income data for comparing living standards.
cards.back:
Even real GDP per capita hides much:

  • Income distribution (an average conceals inequality).
  • The informal economy (subsistence farming, unpaid care, the hidden economy go unrecorded — a big understatement in developing countries).
  • Quality of life (health, leisure, freedom).
  • Negative externalities (polluting output still counts).
  • The composition of output (defence spending raises GDP without raising welfare).
  • Data reliability across countries.

The fullest single comparison is real GDP per capita at PPP; broader indices such as the HDI add health and education.

cards.front: What is purchasing power parity, and why does it matter for international comparisons?
cards.back:
PPP is an exchange rate that equalises the price of an identical basket of goods and services between two countries — what a currency actually buys at home, not what it trades for on foreign exchange markets.

Market rates mislead because they are driven by currency demand and supply, and because non-traded goods — housing, haircuts, restaurant meals — tend to be cheaper in lower-income countries. Comparing incomes at market rates therefore understates living standards in poorer economies.

cards.front: Distinguish nominal from real income, and explain what real national income indicates.
cards.back:
• Nominal income is measured at current prices.
  • Real income strips out inflation, so it reflects what income can actually buy.

Rising real national income is the key indicator of economic performance: it means the economy is genuinely producing more, not just charging higher prices for the same output.

cards.front: Draw the circular flow of income for a simple two-agent economy.
cards.back:
Households and firms are linked by two pairs of flows.

Real flows: households provide the factors of production — land, labour, capital, enterprise — and firms provide goods and services.

Money flows: firms pay income — rent, wages, interest, profit — and households return it as consumer expenditure, which becomes firms' revenue.

The same flow measured at any point gives income = output = expenditure.
cards.svgAlt: Circular flow between firms and households: factors of production and expenditure flow to firms, goods and services and income flow to households

cards.front: Distinguish injections from withdrawals, and state the equilibrium condition.
cards.back:
• Injections — investment, government spending, exports — add new spending to the circular flow.
  • Withdrawals — savings, taxation, imports — leak income out of it.

National income is in equilibrium when injections equal withdrawals; if injections exceed withdrawals the flow expands, and if withdrawals exceed injections it contracts.

Full employment income is the level of national income at which all resources are fully employed — equilibrium need not occur there.

cards.front: Define aggregate demand, and give the relative importance of its components.
cards.back:
Aggregate demand is the total demand for all goods and services in an economy at a given average price level and in a given time period: AD = C + I + G + (X − M).

  • Consumption is the largest component at around 60% of AD.
  • Government spending around 25%.
  • Investment around 14% — the most volatile.
  • Net exports are small and often negative for the UK.

cards.front: What causes a movement along the AD curve?
cards.back:
Only a change in the average price level: a fall from PL1 to PL2 moves the economy along the curve from A to B, raising real GDP demanded from Y1 to Y2 — the inverse relationship the downward slope shows.

Any change in a determinant of AD other than the price level shifts the whole curve instead.
cards.svgAlt: Downward-sloping AD curve with a movement from point A at price level PL1 and output Y1 to point B at PL2 and Y2

cards.front: Show a shift of the AD curve, and name what causes one.
cards.back:
A change in any determinant of AD other than the price level — consumer or business confidence, interest rates, government policy, incomes abroad — changes total planned spending at every price level, shifting the curve (AD1 to AD2 for an increase, back for a decrease).

At the unchanged price level PL, real GDP demanded rises from Y1 to Y2.
cards.svgAlt: Aggregate demand curve shifting right from AD1 to AD2, raising real GDP from Y1 to Y2 at price level PL

cards.front: Use an AD/AS diagram to show macroeconomic equilibrium below full employment.
cards.back:
Short-run equilibrium is where AD crosses SRAS — here at output Y1 and price level PL1. With the LRAS curve at Yfe to the right, this equilibrium leaves a negative output gap: the economy is in balance, but below its full-employment output.

This is the AQA-required use of AD/AS analysis: reading off output and the price level, then judging the position against LRAS.
cards.svgAlt: AD and SRAS intersecting at output Y1 and price level PL1, left of the vertical LRAS curve at Yfe

cards.front: How do demand-side and supply-side shocks affect the macroeconomy?
cards.back:
A demand-side shock — a financial crisis collapsing confidence, a slump in export markets — shifts AD suddenly: output and the price level move in the same direction.

A supply-side shock — an oil price spike, a pandemic disrupting production — shifts SRAS: output and the price level move in opposite directions, the harder case for policy. Global events reach the domestic economy through both routes.

cards.front: What determines consumption, and how are MPC and MPS related?
cards.back:
Consumption — household spending on goods and services, the largest component of AD — is determined primarily by disposable income: income after direct taxes plus transfer payments.

Extra disposable income splits between spending and saving:

  • The MPC is the proportion spent.
  • The MPS is the proportion saved.

So MPC + MPS = 1. Spend £80 of an extra £100 and your MPC is 0.8.

cards.front: Beyond income, what influences consumption and saving?
cards.back:
• Interest rates — higher rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, cutting consumption and raising saving.
  • Confidence — optimism about future income increases spending and borrowing; pessimism increases precautionary saving.
  • Wealth effects — rising house or share prices make households spend more; falling wealth does the reverse.

The determinants of saving are the mirror image of the determinants of consumption — the same forces push the two shares in opposite directions.

cards.front: Distinguish gross from net investment, and saving from investment.
cards.back:
Investment is spending by firms on capital goods.

Depreciation is the loss of value of capital goods over time due to wear and tear or obsolescence — so net investment = gross investment − depreciation: only net investment expands the capital stock.

In economics saving is not investment: saving is household income not spent; investment is firms' spending on capital. The financial sector channels one into the other.

cards.front: Explain the accelerator effect.
cards.back:
The accelerator effect is the idea that a rise in the rate of economic growth results in a larger percentage rise in investment: firms invest in new capital to meet higher expected demand, and that investment further boosts AD and growth.

It works in reverse too — a slowdown in growth produces a larger percentage fall in investment, which is part of why investment is the most volatile component of AD. AQA does not require accelerator calculations.

cards.front: Define the multiplier, and state the multiplier ratio.
cards.back:
The multiplier is the process by which an initial injection, such as an increase in government spending, investment, or exports, leads to a larger final increase in national income and real GDP: the injection becomes income, a proportion is spent (per the MPC), becomes further income, and so on.

The ratio: k = final change in real GDP ÷ initial injection.

A £2bn injection producing a £6bn rise in GDP means k = 3.

cards.front: How does AQA require you to calculate the multiplier, and why does the MPC set its size?
cards.back:
From the MPC only: if MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4. (AQA states that calculations from the marginal propensities to withdraw will not be expected — that is Edexcel territory.)

The MPC governs the magnitude because it fixes how much of each round of income is re-spent: a higher MPC means less leaks away each round, so the rounds shrink more slowly and the total effect is larger.
cards.formulaHtml: M=1/(1−MPC)M = 1/(1 - MPC)M=1/(1−MPC)

cards.front: Show the multiplier effect on an AD/AS diagram.
cards.back:
The initial injection shifts AD from AD1 to AD2; the induced rounds of consumer spending carry it further to AD3. Real GDP rises from Y1 to Y2 and then Y3 — a total rise larger than the initial injection alone would give.

As the economy climbs towards capacity, more of each shift feeds the price level (PL1 to PL3) and less feeds output — the multiplier is most powerful with spare capacity.
cards.svgAlt: AD shifting right from AD1 to AD2 and then AD3 along a Keynesian LRAS1 curve, raising real GDP from Y1 to Y2 to Y3 and the price level from PL1 to PL3

cards.front: Define SRAS, and name the cost changes that shift it.
cards.back:
Short-run aggregate supply is the total planned output of goods and services in an economy at a given price level, assuming that at least one factor of production, such as capital or technology, is fixed. It slopes upward because higher output brings rising unit costs, so firms need higher prices.

The named shift factors:

  • Money wage rates.
  • Raw material prices.
  • Business taxation.
  • Productivity.

Anything changing production costs across the economy.

cards.front: Show the effect of a fall in production costs on SRAS.
cards.back:
SRAS shifts right (SRAS1 to SRAS2): firms supply more at every given price level, so at the unchanged price level PL output rises from Y1 to Y2.

Causes:

  • Lower money wage rates.
  • Cheaper raw materials.
  • Lighter business taxation.
  • Higher productivity.

Rising costs shift the curve left instead — the anatomy of a supply-side shock.
cards.svgAlt: SRAS1 shifting right to SRAS2, raising real GDP supplied from Y1 to Y2 at the unchanged price level PL

cards.front: Define LRAS, and what the position of the vertical curve represents.
cards.back:
Long-run aggregate supply is the total potential output of an economy when all factors of production are fully and efficiently employed — the economy's productive capacity.

The position of the vertical LRAS curve represents the normal capacity level of output; shifts in LRAS are long-run growth or decline, equivalent to the PPF moving.

cards.front: Name AQA's fundamental determinants of LRAS.
cards.back:
Technology, productivity, attitudes, enterprise, factor mobility and economic incentives — the AQA list is broader than a factors-of-production checklist, reaching into how willing and able an economy is to use what it has.

AQA also stresses the institutional structure of the economy — notably a banking system that channels funds into business investment — as a determinant of aggregate supply.

cards.front: Draw and explain the Keynesian AS curve.
cards.back:
An L-shaped curve with three phases:

  • Perfectly elastic at low output, where spare capacity lets firms expand without raising prices.
  • Upward sloping as resources grow scarce.
  • Vertical at full capacity Yfe, where extra demand only raises prices.

It embodies the Keynesian belief that the economy can sit below full employment for a long time.
cards.svgAlt: L-shaped Keynesian LRAS curve: flat at low output, sloping upward as capacity nears, vertical at full-capacity output Yfe

cards.front: Show underlying economic growth on an AD/AS diagram.
cards.back:
Underlying (long-run) growth is a rightward shift of the LRAS curve, from LRAS1 to LRAS2: normal capacity output rises from Yfe1 to Yfe2.

It is driven by the fundamental determinants — technology, productivity, enterprise, factor mobility, incentives — improving the quantity or quality of what the economy can produce.
cards.svgAlt: Vertical LRAS1 curve shifting right to LRAS2, raising full-employment output from Yfe1 to Yfe2

cards.front: Distinguish short-run from long-run growth, and their determinants.
cards.back:
Short-run (actual) growth — a rise in real GDP, caused by an increase in AD (any of C, I, G, X − M) or in SRAS through lower production costs. The economy moves closer to its existing potential.

Long-run growth — a rise in productive capacity, the trend rate of growth of real national output over time; on diagrams, LRAS and the PPF shift outward.

cards.front: Draw the economic cycle, and name the indicators that identify its phases.
cards.back:
Actual real GDP fluctuates around the rising trend rate of growth: boom above trend, then downturn, recession below trend, then recovery.

To place an economy in the cycle, read a range of indicators together:

  • Real GDP growth.
  • Inflation.
  • Unemployment.
  • Investment.

Booms pair fast growth with rising inflation and investment; recessions the reverse.
cards.svgAlt: Real GDP fluctuating around a rising trend line, above it in a boom and below it in a recession, with downturn and recovery marked

cards.front: Show a positive output gap, and its meaning.
cards.back:
AD and SRAS intersect at Y1, to the right of LRAS at Yfe: real GDP is above the economy's productive potential — overtime, factors overworked — which is what defines a positive output gap.

A negative gap is the mirror case, real GDP below potential. Gap positions map onto the cycle: positive in booms, negative in recessions.
cards.svgAlt: AD and SRAS intersecting at output Y1 right of the vertical LRAS curve at Yfe, showing a positive output gap

cards.front: What causes cyclical instability?
cards.back:
Beyond ordinary demand-side and supply-side shocks — domestic and global — four amplifiers:

  • Excessive growth in credit and debt.
  • Asset price bubbles.
  • Destabilising speculation.
  • Animal spirits or herding, where confidence swings feed on themselves.

Each can turn a shock into a cycle: cheap credit inflates a bubble, herding sustains it, and the correction delivers the downturn.

cards.front: Weigh the costs and benefits of economic growth.
cards.back:
Benefits — higher real incomes and living standards, more employment, higher tax revenue and business investment.

Costs — demand-pull inflation, inequality where gains are uneven, and environmental damage: pollution, emissions, resource depletion.

Be ready with a view on sustainability — whether today's growth compromises the environment and resources future generations depend on.

cards.front: Define unemployed, the labour force and economic inactivity.
cards.back:
Unemployed — of working age, without work, but willing and able to work and actively seeking employment.

The labour force is the total of those in employment and those unemployed who are actively seeking work.

Economically inactive — people of working age not seeking work: full-time students, early retirees, the long-term sick, discouraged workers.

cards.front: Contrast the UK's two measures of unemployment.
cards.back:
The Labour Force Survey (ILO measure) — a household survey counting those without work who are available to start within two weeks and have sought work in the last four weeks; internationally comparable.

The claimant count — the number claiming unemployment-related benefits. The LFS is usually the higher figure, since many who are genuinely unemployed are not eligible for, or do not claim, benefits.

cards.front: Name and define the four types of unemployment.
cards.back:
• Frictional — short-term, between jobs.
  • Structural — a mismatch between workers' skills and available jobs, often from technological change.
  • Seasonal — demand for some labour fluctuates across the year.
  • Cyclical — demand-deficient unemployment in a downturn, linked to a negative output gap.

The cause decides the cure: demand-side policy treats cyclical unemployment; supply-side policy treats structural and frictional.

cards.front: Define real wage unemployment and the natural rate of unemployment.
cards.back:
Real wage unemployment occurs when wages are set above the market-clearing level, leaving an excess supply of labour — possible causes include minimum wage laws and trade union negotiations.

The natural rate of unemployment is the unemployment that remains at full employment: the frictional and structural components that never fully disappear. Supply-side factors set it, and it fixes where LRAS — and the long-run Phillips curve — stand.

cards.front: Evaluate the consequences of unemployment.
cards.back:
For individuals — lower income and living standards, skills and experience decay that makes re-employment harder, and damage to mental and physical health.

For the economy — lost output and lower AD, higher welfare spending and lower tax revenue for the government, and wasted productive potential. The evaluation point: the right policy response depends entirely on the cause — stimulus cures cyclical unemployment but not structural.

cards.front: Define inflation, deflation and disinflation.
cards.back:
Inflation — a sustained increase in the general/average price level of goods and services in an economy.

Deflation — a sustained decrease in the price level: a negative inflation rate.

Disinflation — a fall in the rate of inflation: prices still rising, more slowly.

A common trap: deflationary policies are policies that reduce AD — they do not necessarily cause deflation.

cards.front: Show demand-pull inflation on an AD/AS diagram.
cards.back:
AD shifts right (AD1 to AD2) — rising consumer spending, credit growth, fiscal stimulus — along an unchanged SRAS: the price level rises from PL1 to PL2 as output rises from Y1 to Y2.

Prices are pulled up by excess demand, strongest as the economy nears capacity.
cards.svgAlt: Aggregate demand shifting right from AD1 to AD2 along the SRAS curve, raising the price level from PL1 to PL2 and real GDP from Y1 to Y2

cards.front: Show cost-push inflation, and how world prices feed it.
cards.back:
An economy-wide rise in production costs shifts SRAS left (SRAS1 to SRAS2) along AD: the price level rises from PL1 to PL2 while output falls from Y1 to Y2.

This is the channel for imported inflation: rising world commodity prices — oil, gas, food — and inflation in other economies raise UK firms' costs, so domestic inflation can arrive from abroad.
cards.svgAlt: Short-run aggregate supply shifting left from SRAS1 to SRAS2 along the AD curve, raising the price level from PL1 to PL2 while real GDP falls from Y1 to Y2

cards.front: State Fisher's equation of exchange, and the Quantity Theory of Money.
cards.back:
M is the money supply, V the velocity of circulation, P the price level and Q real output — so PQ is nominal national income.

The Quantity Theory (the monetarist model): if V and Q are stable, growth in the money supply feeds directly into the price level — inflation is "always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon", and controlling the money supply is the key to price stability. Expectations matter too: if people expect inflation, wage and price setting deliver it.
cards.formulaHtml: M×V=P×QM × V = P × QM×V=P×Q

cards.front: Evaluate the consequences of inflation and deflation.
cards.back:
Inflation erodes purchasing power (hitting fixed incomes hardest), erodes savings, creates uncertainty that deters investment, and harms competitiveness if UK prices rise faster than rivals'.

Deflation can be worse: households delay spending expecting lower prices, the real burden of debt rises, and falling revenues force firms to cut jobs — a self-reinforcing spiral. Low and stable inflation, not zero, is the target for a reason.

cards.front: How do output gaps relate to unemployment and inflationary pressure?
cards.back:
A negative output gap means spare capacity: cyclical unemployment rises and inflationary pressure eases. A positive output gap means the economy is straining beyond potential: unemployment is low but demand-pull inflation builds.

This single mechanism underlies most objective conflicts — policy that closes one gap usually opens pressure somewhere else, at least in the short run.

cards.front: Draw and explain the short-run Phillips curve.
cards.back:
The SRPC shows a short-run trade-off between unemployment and inflation: lower unemployment raises incomes and spending, bidding prices up (demand-pull).

Policy reading: demand management can buy lower unemployment at the price of higher inflation — but only in the short run, while inflation expectations lag behind actual inflation.
cards.svgAlt: Short-run Phillips curve convex to the origin, showing lower unemployment paired with higher inflation

cards.front: Draw and explain the long-run Phillips curve.
cards.back:
In the long run the Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment: expectations adjust to actual inflation, so stimulating demand just shifts the short-run curve up (SRPC1 to SRPC2) — same unemployment, higher inflation (2% to 5%).

The monetarist/supply-side conclusion: no long-run trade-off, so the objectives are compatible in the long run — demand policy should target inflation, and only supply-side policy can lower the NRU itself.
cards.svgAlt: Vertical long-run Phillips curve at the natural rate of unemployment, crossed by SRPC1 at 2 percent inflation and the higher SRPC2 at 5 percent

cards.front: What are the functions and characteristics of money?
cards.back:
Four functions:

  • A medium of exchange.
  • A unit of account for comparing value.
  • A store of value for deferring consumption.
  • A standard of deferred payment for settling debts over time.

Six characteristics make something work as money:

  • Durability.
  • Portability.
  • Divisibility.
  • Uniformity.
  • Acceptability.
  • Limited supply — the last is what protects its value from inflation.

cards.front: Define the money supply — and distinguish narrow money from broad money.
cards.back:
Money supply: the total amount of money available in an economy at a particular point in time.

  • Narrow money (M1): the most liquid forms — cash and demand deposits, readily available for transactions.
  • Broad money (M2, M3…): narrow money plus less liquid forms such as savings accounts and time deposits — the total money supply, liquid and less liquid alike.

cards.front: Distinguish the money market, the capital market and the foreign exchange market.
cards.back:
• The money market: short-term borrowing and lending, typically a year or less — how firms and governments manage short-term funding.
  • The capital market: long-term borrowing and lending beyond a year — where bonds and shares raise capital for investment and expansion.
  • The foreign exchange market: where currencies are bought and sold, letting firms manage exchange-rate risk.

Together they channel savings into investment across the wider economy.

cards.front: Distinguish debt from equity as ways for a firm to raise finance.
cards.back:
Debt: borrowed funds — bank loans or corporate bonds — that must be repaid with interest. Interest is tax-deductible and ownership is not diluted, and debt can be the cheaper source of finance.

Equity: funds raised by issuing shares. Shareholders become part-owners entitled to dividends from profits — no repayment obligation, a long-term source of capital, but ownership is diluted. Firms raise finance by issuing shares, issuing corporate bonds, or borrowing from a bank.

cards.front: Define a bond, its coupon and maturity — and state the yield formula.
cards.back:
Bond: a tradable debt security issued by a government or a firm in order to borrow money — UK government bonds are gilts.

  • The coupon is the fixed annual interest payment as a percentage of the £100 face value.
  • Maturity is the date the face value is repaid in one lump sum.

Bond yield (%) = annual coupon payment ÷ market price × 100. The coupon is fixed, so when the market price falls the yield rises — and vice versa.

cards.front: A gilt has a £100 face value and a 4% coupon. Calculate its yield at a market price of £80 and at £160 — what does this show?
cards.back:
The coupon is fixed at £4 a year. At £80: 4 ÷ 80 × 100 = 5%. At £160: 4 ÷ 160 × 100 = 2.5%.

The inverse relationship between bond prices and yields: the same £4 is a bigger return on a cheaper bond. When market interest rates rise, existing bonds' fixed coupons look unattractive, their prices fall — and their yields rise to match the market.

cards.front: Distinguish a commercial bank from an investment bank.
cards.back:
Commercial bank: a bank that accepts deposits from households and firms, makes loans to them, and provides a payments system — profiting from the interest rate spread.

Its three functions:

  • Accepting deposits (sight and time accounts).
  • Lending.
  • Providing a payments mechanism.

Investment bank: takes no public deposits; it underwrites share and bond issues, advises on takeovers and trades securities for large firms, governments and institutions — higher risk, funded from wholesale markets.

Many banks do both, which raises systemic risk.

cards.front: Describe the structure of a commercial bank's balance sheet.
cards.back:
Assets = Liabilities + Capital, always.

  • Deposits are liabilities — the bank owes them back to customers.
  • Loans are assets — borrowers owe them to the bank.

Getting that backwards is the classic error.

Liabilities: customer deposits (largest), bonds issued and wholesale borrowing.

Assets, in descending order of liquidity: cash and central-bank balances, bills, then loans and advances — the least liquid but most profitable, and normally the largest.

cards.front: What are a commercial bank's three objectives — and how do they conflict?
cards.back:
• Liquidity (meet withdrawals on demand — survival).
  • Profitability (maximise returns for shareholders).
  • Security (minimise losses from bad debts).

The central conflict is liquidity vs profitability: the most liquid assets earn the least, the most profitable are the least liquid — too little liquidity risks a bank run, too much sacrifices profit.

And profitability vs security: higher returns come only from riskier lending, whose defaults can wipe out the bank's capital.

cards.front: How do banks create credit?
cards.back:
Credit creation: the process by which commercial banks make loans that create new bank deposits, thereby increasing the money supply.

A new loan credits the borrower's account with a new deposit — banks do not merely lend out savers' money.

It rests on fractional reserve banking: only a fraction of deposits is ever withdrawn at once, so banks hold a fraction as reserves and lend the rest; each loan becomes someone else's deposit and the cycle repeats, multiplying deposits.

Credit growth drives AD — and excessive growth feeds inflation and asset bubbles.

cards.front: Define a central bank — and its main functions.
cards.back:
Central bank: a national bank that provides financial and banking services for a country's government and commercial banks — in the UK, the Bank of England.

Its functions:

  • Issuing currency.
  • Managing the money supply.
  • Setting interest rates.
  • Acting as lender of last resort in crises.
  • Regulating and supervising banks.

cards.front: How does a cut in interest rates feed through to aggregate demand?
cards.back:
The MPC's rate changes reach AD through three channels:

  • Consumption: cheaper borrowing, less reward for saving, and variable-rate mortgage holders keep more disposable income.
  • Investment: firms' cost of borrowing falls, so more projects pay.
  • Net exports: lower returns send hot money abroad, the extra supply of pounds depreciates the currency, exports cheapen and imports dearen.

All three raise AD — and a rate rise runs the whole mechanism in reverse.

cards.front: Show the impact of expansionary monetary policy on the AQA macro objectives.
cards.back:
AD shifts right from AD1 to AD2: real GDP rises Y1 to Y2 and the price level PL1 to PL2 — growth up, unemployment down (derived demand for labour), inflation up; the weaker pound helps net trade. On the classical curve at full employment, the same shift raises only the price level.

Watch the distribution effects: cheap money inflates asset prices, favouring the asset-rich — and higher consumption strains environmental sustainability.
cards.svgAlt: Keynesian AS curve with aggregate demand shifting right from AD1 to AD2, raising real GDP from Y1 to Y2 and the price level from PL1 to PL2 below full employment output Yfe

cards.front: How does quantitative easing work — and name the four channels of the transmission mechanism.
cards.back:
QE: the central bank creates new money and buys government bonds from financial institutions; the banks' liquidity rises, so to lend it out they cut commercial interest rates — and the lower rates stimulate C, I and (X−M) just as a Bank Rate cut would.

The transmission mechanism's four channels: the interest rate channel, the credit channel (availability of lending), the exchange rate channel (hot money and the currency), and the asset price channel (wealth effects on consumption).

cards.front: Evaluate the effectiveness of interest rate cuts and QE.
cards.back:
• Time lags — effects can take up to two years; fixed-rate borrowers feel nothing at first.
  • The liquidity trap — near the zero lower bound, further cuts change little, which is why QE exists at all.
  • Asset price bubbles — cheap money inflates housing and shares, and bursting bubbles bring crises.
  • Confidence — in a recession, households save the windfall and firms delay investment regardless of the rate.

Monetary policy pulls on a string it cannot push.

cards.front: Who regulates the UK financial system — and what does each body do?
cards.back:
Within the Bank of England: the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) sets capital and liquidity standards for individual banks and runs stress tests; the Financial Policy Committee (FPC) watches the whole system, deploying macroprudential tools such as loan-to-value limits.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) polices conduct: protecting consumers, promoting competition, and holding institutions to rules on fair treatment and disclosure.

cards.front: Define the liquidity ratio and capital ratio — and which failure does each guard against?
cards.back:
Liquidity ratio: the proportion of a bank's assets that are held in liquid form, such as cash, reserves at the central bank and easily marketable securities — liquid assets ÷ total assets × 100.

It guards against illiquidity: being unable to meet withdrawals, the bank-run failure of borrowing short and lending long.

Capital ratio: capital ÷ risk-weighted assets × 100.

Capital absorbs losses when borrowers default; once losses exceed it, the bank is insolvent.

cards.front: Explain systemic risk and moral hazard — and why regulating them involves a trade-off.
cards.back:
Systemic risk: the risk that the failure of one financial institution triggers the failure of others and a wider financial crisis — interbank lending, shared assets and confidence spread failure by contagion (Lehman Brothers, 2008).

Moral hazard: too-big-to-fail banks take excessive risks expecting bailouts (RBS and Lloyds).

The trade-off: the tools that contain systemic risk — deposit insurance, lender of last resort, bailouts — are the very tools that create moral hazard; and the capital and liquidity rules that make banks safer also restrict credit creation and growth.

Regulators can fully eliminate neither risk.

cards.front: Define fiscal policy, and its expansionary and contractionary forms.
cards.back:
Fiscal policy is the government's manipulation of government spending (G) and taxation (T) to meet macroeconomic objectives — with microeconomic functions too, such as correcting market failures and changing incentives.

  • Expansionary: raise G, cut T — AD rises.
  • Contractionary: cut G, raise T — AD falls.

Spending on education, infrastructure and R&D also works on the supply side, shifting LRAS.

cards.front: Distinguish the types of public expenditure, and why governments levy taxes.
cards.back:
• Current expenditure — day-to-day spending on public-sector wages and consumables (teachers' pay, medicines).
  • Capital expenditure — long-term investment in assets such as infrastructure.
  • Transfer payments — payments with no output in return, such as benefits and pensions (excluded from G in AD).

Taxes exist to fund this spending, manage AD, correct market failures and redistribute income.

cards.front: Distinguish progressive, proportional and regressive taxes.
cards.back:
• Progressive — the average tax rate rises with income (UK income tax).
  • Proportional — the same rate at every income.
  • Regressive — the average rate falls as income rises, taking a bigger share from the poor (duties, VAT in practice).

The principles of taxation ask taxes to be equitable, efficient, certain and convenient — the mix of direct taxes (on income and profits) and indirect taxes (on spending) is judged against these.

cards.front: Distinguish the deficit from the debt, and cyclical from structural deficits — and what is the OBR?
cards.back:
The fiscal deficit is one year's gap between spending and tax revenue; the national debt is the accumulation of past deficits. A cyclical deficit widens in recessions and narrows in booms as revenue and welfare spending swing; a structural deficit persists even at potential output — the harder problem, unfixed by growth.

The Office for Budget Responsibility provides independent forecasts of the public finances, monitors fiscal policy, and publishes analysis that keeps governments transparent and accountable.

cards.front: Draw and explain the Laffer curve.
cards.back:
Total tax revenue against the tax rate: revenue is zero at 0% (nothing taxed) and at 100% (no incentive to earn), so revenue is maximised at some intermediate rate. Beyond it, higher rates reduce revenue — the higher rate t2 raises less (R2) than the lower rate t1 does (R1) — because incentives to work and invest shrink and avoidance grows.

A strong evaluation of any tax rise: the revenue gain assumes behaviour does not change.
cards.svgAlt: Dome-shaped Laffer curve of tax revenue against the tax rate, with revenue R1 at rate t1 higher than revenue R2 at the higher rate t2

cards.front: Distinguish supply-side policies from supply-side improvements.
cards.back:
Supply-side policies are government measures to raise the economy's productive potential, shifting LRAS right.

Supply-side improvements are the capacity gains themselves — and they often originate in the private sector, through productivity gains, innovation and investment, independently of government.

Policy divides into market-based (removing intervention) and interventionist (government spending) approaches.

cards.front: Give examples of free-market and interventionist supply-side policies, and their effect on the natural rate.
cards.back:
• Free-market: tax cuts to sharpen incentives, privatisation, deregulation, labour-market reforms.
  • Interventionist: government spending on education and training, industrial policy, subsidising research and development.

By improving skills, mobility and incentives, both routes can lower the natural rate of unemployment — the frictional and structural core that demand policy cannot touch — while raising potential output and the trend growth rate.

cards.front: Show the effect of successful supply-side policy, and its reach across the objectives.
cards.back:
LRAS shifts right (LRAS1 to LRAS2): output rises from Yfe1 to Yfe2 while the price level falls — growth without inflation.

That reach is the appeal: more output, downward price pressure, a lower natural rate of unemployment, and stronger competitiveness improving the current account. The costs are time and — for interventionist policies — money.
cards.svgAlt: Vertical LRAS1 shifting right to LRAS2 along a downward-sloping AD curve, raising output from Yfe1 to Yfe2 and lowering the price level from PL1 to PL2

cards.front: Define globalisation — and what characterises it?
cards.back:
Globalisation: the increasing integration and interdependence of the world's economies.

Its characteristics: increased free trade in goods and services across borders; increased foreign direct investment (FDI) and capital flows; increased foreign ownership of firms through multinational and transnational corporations; and increased freedom of movement of labour between countries.

cards.front: What has driven globalisation over the last 50 years?
cards.back:
• Trade liberalisation — falling tariffs and quotas (China's WTO entry in 2001 transformed its trade).
  • Advances in transport and communication technology.
  • The growth of MNCs building global supply chains (Apple, Amazon, Unilever).
  • Containerisation, which slashed shipping costs and time.
  • The deregulation of financial markets in the 1990s freeing capital flows.
  • Global institutions — the WTO, IMF and World Bank — promoting free trade and investment.

cards.front: Evaluate the consequences of globalisation across its stakeholders.
cards.back:
• Consumers: lower prices, more variety and quality — against cultural imperialism and import-quality concerns.
  • Workers: jobs and rising wages in developing countries — against job losses where production relocates.
  • Firms: bigger markets, cheaper inputs and economies of scale — against fiercer competition and fragile supply chains.
  • Governments: growth and tax revenue — against inequality and exposure to external shocks.
  • The environment mostly loses: more production, transport, emissions and resource exploitation.

cards.front: Distinguish absolute advantage from comparative advantage.
cards.back:
Absolute advantage: a country can produce more of a good with the same resources than another country — productivity and efficiency.

Comparative advantage: a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country. The theory says countries should specialise where their opportunity cost is lowest — raising the efficiency of resource allocation and total global output.

cards.front: Show comparative advantage using two countries' PPFs.
cards.back:
Germany's PPF runs from 150mn T-shirts to 20mn chips; Vietnam's from 200mn T-shirts to 10mn chips — each has an absolute advantage in one good.

Opportunity costs:

  • A chip costs Germany 7.5 T-shirts but Vietnam 20.
  • A T-shirt costs Vietnam 0.05 chips but Germany 0.13.

Each specialises where its opportunity cost is lower: fully specialised, they produce 20m chips and 200mn T-shirts — beating the 15m and 175mn made without specialisation — and by trading, both consume beyond their own PPFs.
cards.svgAlt: Two straight-line PPFs for computer chips and T-shirts crossing on shared axes: Germany's runs from 150 million T-shirts to 20 million chips, Vietnam's from 200 million T-shirts to 10 million chips

cards.front: What are the benefits and costs of international trade — and what changes the pattern of trade?
cards.back:
Benefits

  • Efficiency from specialising at lower opportunity cost.
  • Higher global output.
  • Lower prices.
  • Greater variety.
  • Economies of scale and growth.

Costs

  • Import dependency.
  • Job losses in uncompetitive industries.
  • Inequality.
  • Environmental damage.
  • Worker exploitation where standards are low.

The pattern of trade — what is traded and with whom — shifts with comparative advantage (UK manufacturing's decline), emerging economies, trade blocs and agreements (Brexit), and relative exchange rates.

cards.front: Show the impact of a tariff — prices, quantities and the three areas.
cards.back:
The tariff lifts the world supply price from P1 (Sworld) to P2 (Sworld+tariff): domestic output extends from Q1 to Q2, consumption contracts from Q4 to Q3, and imports shrink from Q4 − Q1 to Q3 − Q2.

The green area is the gain in domestic producer surplus, the purple rectangle is government tariff revenue, and the two red triangles are the net welfare loss. Protection's other faces — quotas, subsidies to domestic producers, non-tariff barriers — shift the same surpluses without the revenue.
cards.svgAlt: Tariff diagram with domestic supply and demand and two horizontal world supply lines: the tariff raises the price from P1 to P2, with a green producer surplus gain, a purple tariff revenue rectangle and two red welfare loss triangles

cards.front: Why do countries turn to protectionism — and with what consequences?
cards.back:
Reasons: protecting infant, strategic and sunset industries and the jobs in them; preventing dumping; improving the balance of payments; and enforcing environmental and labour standards.

Consequences: higher consumer prices and restricted choice, retaliation escalating into trade wars, and sheltered inefficiency — protection blunts the incentives to innovate. Its bite also depends on import demand elasticity and whether domestic producers can actually expand.

cards.front: What is a customs union — and what are trade creation, trade diversion and the WTO's role?
cards.back:
A customs union (e.g. MERCOSUR) removes tariffs and quotas between members and adds a common external tariff; a free trade area lacks the common tariff, a common market (the EU) adds free movement of labour and capital.

Trade creation: trade shifts to a lower-cost producer inside the bloc — welfare rises.

Trade diversion: it shifts from a cheaper outsider to a dearer member — welfare falls.

The WTO promotes trade liberalisation as negotiating forum and dispute court — in tension with blocs that favour their members.

cards.front: Define the balance of payments — and what does each account record?
cards.back:
Balance of payments (BoP): records all financial transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Inflows are credits, outflows debits.

  • The current account: trade in goods and services, primary income (profits, interest, dividends) and secondary income (aid, remittances).
  • The capital account: minor capital transfers such as debt forgiveness.
  • The financial account: FDI, portfolio investment and reserve changes.

Since the BoP must balance, a current account deficit is financed by a capital and financial account surplus.

cards.front: A country records: trade in goods — credits £240bn, debits £330bn; services — £280bn, £205bn; primary income — £55bn, £70bn; secondary income — £30bn, £40bn. Calculate the current account balance.
cards.back:
• Goods: 240 − 330 = −£90bn
  • Services: 280 − 205 = +£75bn
  • Primary income: 55 − 70 = −£15bn
  • Secondary income: 30 − 40 = −£10bn

Balance: −90 + 75 − 15 − 10 = −£40bn — a current account deficit, with the services surplus offsetting more than half the goods deficit.

Always net all four components.

cards.front: What causes a current account deficit — and why do persistent imbalances matter?
cards.back:
Causes:

  • Low competitiveness (weak productivity or high inflation against rivals).
  • A strong exchange rate.
  • High domestic demand sucking in imports.
  • Structural decline such as a shrinking manufacturing base.

Persistent deficits build foreign debt and can trigger currency depreciation and weaker FDI as confidence erodes.

Persistent surpluses feed inflation and over-reliance on exports, leaving the economy exposed to global downturns.

cards.front: Evaluate the three policy routes for correcting a current account deficit.
cards.back:
• Expenditure-switching (tariffs, quotas, devaluation) redirects demand towards domestic output — quick, but invites retaliation and raises consumer prices.
  • Expenditure-reducing (contractionary fiscal policy, higher interest rates) cuts demand and imports together — at the price of slower growth and higher unemployment.
  • Supply-side policies (education, R&D, infrastructure) rebuild export competitiveness — the durable fix, but slow and costly.

Each route trades the current account against other macro objectives.

cards.front: Compare floating and fixed exchange rate systems.
cards.back:
Floating: an exchange rate system determined by market forces of demand and supply for a currency, with no government intervention. For: automatic current-account adjustment, monetary policy freed for domestic goals, no costly intervention. Against: volatility deters trade and investment, depreciation imports inflation, speculation.

Fixed: the central bank holds a set value by buying or selling currency and moving interest rates. For: stability for trade and investment, less imported inflation and speculation. Against: costly intervention, monetary policy captured by the peg, and over- or under-valuation distorting trade.

cards.front: Show what makes a floating currency appreciate — and what moves the demand and supply of it.
cards.back:
Higher demand for the currency shifts D1 right to D2 along the supply curve: the exchange rate rises from P1 to P2.

Demand rises with:

  • Higher relative interest rates (hot money).
  • Lower relative inflation.
  • A current account surplus.
  • FDI inflows.
  • Bullish speculation.

Supply moves it the other way: QE and speculative selling expand the currency's supply and depreciate it.
cards.svgAlt: Currency market diagram with demand for the currency shifting right from D1 to D2 along a fixed supply curve, raising the exchange rate from P1 to P2

cards.front: Show the J-curve — and state the Marshall-Lerner condition.
cards.back:
After a depreciation the current account worsens first: contracts fix prices in the short run and consumers are slow to switch, so PEDx and PEDm are inelastic.

Only as they adjust does the balance improve through the long run — tracing a J.

The Marshall-Lerner condition: a depreciation improves the current account only if PEDx + PEDm > 1. If combined demand is inelastic, it worsens instead.
cards.svgAlt: J-curve diagram of the net trade balance against time: after a depreciation the deficit deepens in the short run, bottoms out, then improves into surplus in the long run

cards.front: What makes a currency union succeed — and what does membership cost?
cards.back:
A currency union (the Eurozone) adds a single currency to a common market. Success needs:

  • Synchronised business cycles.
  • Labour mobility.
  • Fiscal transfers to cushion shocked regions.
  • Mobility of capital.

For members:

  • Lower transaction costs.
  • Price transparency.
  • More trade and investment.
  • No exchange-rate risk.

Against: the loss of independent monetary policy and exchange-rate flexibility — leaving members exposed when asymmetric shocks hit.

cards.front: Distinguish growth from development — and how is development measured?
cards.back:
Economic growth: the narrower concept, measured by rises in real GDP.

Economic development: a broader concept. It includes economic growth but also considers improvements in living standards, welfare, and quality of life.

Measures:

  • Single indicators (infant mortality, literacy) give partial pictures.
  • Composite indicators combine them — the UN's HDI weights health (life expectancy), education (schooling years) and income (real GNI per capita at PPP) equally, scoring 0 to 1.

cards.front: Evaluate the HDI as a measure of development.
cards.back:
For: a composite measure capturing more than income; enables international comparisons; puts health and education alongside GDP.

Against: it hides inequality within countries; ignores sustainability and the environment; and rests on data quality that is often unreliable in developing countries. Alternatives fill the gaps — the MPI, the inequality-adjusted IHDI, and environmental indicators.

cards.front: What are the main barriers to growth and development?
cards.back:
Economic

  • Primary product dependency (volatile prices, Dutch disease).
  • The savings gap — the Harrod-Domar model ties growth to savings and investment.
  • The foreign currency gap and capital flight.
  • Demographics and debt servicing.
  • Poor access to credit and weak infrastructure.
  • Inadequate education and skills, and the absence of property rights, which kills the incentive to invest.

Non-economic: corruption, poor governance and instability, conflict, and geography.

cards.front: Compare market-orientated and interventionist strategies for development — and the role of aid.
cards.back:
Market-orientated — free market forces drive development:

  • Trade liberalisation.
  • FDI promotion.
  • Subsidy removal.
  • Floating exchange rates.
  • Microfinance.
  • Privatisation.

Interventionist — the state corrects market failure:

  • Human capital investment.
  • Protectionism.
  • Managed exchange rates.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Joint ventures.
  • Buffer stocks.

Aid comes in three forms:

  • Humanitarian aid (emergency relief).
  • Debt relief (freeing resources for investment).
  • Official Development Assistance — soft loans and grants, effective unless dependency or corruption blunts them.

cards.front: Show how a buffer stock scheme stabilises a commodity price.
cards.back:
The scheme defends a band between Pmax and Pmin. In a normal year S1 sets P1 inside the band. A good harvest (S2) would push the price to P2, below the floor — so the scheme buys stock. A bad harvest (S3) would send the price to P3, above the ceiling — so it sells stock.

Stable prices smooth farm incomes and encourage investment — if the scheme can afford the stockpile and sets the band well.
cards.svgAlt: Commodity market diagram with demand, three supply curves and a price band: a good harvest pushes the price below the floor so the scheme buys stock, a bad harvest pushes it above the ceiling so the scheme sells, keeping the price between Pmax and Pmin
